keyVerseText: And to every beast of the earth, and to every fowl of the air, and to every thing that creepeth upon the earth, wherein there is life , I have given every green herb for meat: and it was so. life: Heb. a living soul
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun יֶרֶק (yereq) derives from the root יָרָק (yârâq), which primarily means 'to spit,' an idiom linked to a vacuity or absence of color. This etymology suggests a transition from a sense of emptiness or pallor to the visible green hue associated with vegetation. Thus, the root meaning enriches the common English gloss of 'grass' or 'green thing' by emphasizing the color's distinctiveness as a sign of life and vitality emerging from barrenness or dullness.
usageInScripture: The word יֶרֶק (yereq) appears six times in Scripture, consistently referring to green plants, grass, or verdure. Translations such as 'the grass,' 'every green,' and 'not any green thing' reflect its use to denote living, green vegetation essential for sustaining animal life. This consistent semantic range highlights its concrete meaning as the greenery of the earth, including both herbaceous plants and sometimes encompassing trees, as seen in its use in Genesis 1:30 and other passages.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding יֶרֶק (yereq) as the green vegetation God created underscores His provision for all living creatures, affirming His sovereignty over creation. The green plants symbolize life and sustenance, given by God to animals as food, reflecting His care and the orderliness of His creation. This word also points to the vitality and renewal inherent in God's design, reminding believers that God sustains life through His provision. The green color, rooted in a contrast to emptiness or pallor, metaphorically invites reflection on spiritual vitality found in Christ, who brings life where there was barrenness.
keyVerseReflection: Genesis 1:30 states, 'And to every beast of the earth, and to every fowl of the air, and to every thing that creepeth upon the earth, wherein there is life, I have given every green herb for meat.' Here, יֶרֶק (yereq) emphasizes the green plants as the divinely appointed sustenance for all living creatures. The word highlights the provision and order God established at creation, ensuring that all life is supported by the green vegetation He created. This verse reveals God's intentional care in supplying life with what it needs, with יֶרֶק symbolizing the tangible expression of His sustaining grace.
